{
  "hypothesis": "Predicted that retrieval accuracy for different associations within the same event would be mutually contingent, indicating holistic recollection, and that the degree of this dependency would increase from age 4 to adulthood.",
  "design": "mixed, with age (4-year-olds, 6-year-olds, young adults) as a between-subjects factor and retrieval dependency as a within-subjects measure.",
  "manipulation_or_predictor": "Age (4-year-olds, 6-year-olds, young adults) and the within-event contingency of retrieval success.",
  "outcome_measure": "Retrieval dependency, calculated as the difference between the observed proportion of joint retrieval (accuracy for multiple associations within the same event) and the proportion predicted by an independent model.",
  "population_and_setting": "4-year-olds, 6-year-olds, and young adults recruited from the Philadelphia suburban area and Temple University.",
  "sample_size_total": 93,
  "recruitment_and_incentive": "Children received a small toy; adults received partial course credit.",
  "analysis_plan": "One-sample t-tests to determine if dependency exceeded zero for each age group, and a one-way ANOVA to compare the magnitude of dependency across age groups.",
  "preregistered_or_confirmatory": "not stated",
  "other_methods_notes": "Participants learned multi-element events (scene, person, object). Children's task included a narrative at encoding; adults' task did not. Dependency was computed by comparing observed joint retrieval to an independent model baseline."
}
